records.central_bank: Centrale Bank van Curaçao en Sint Maarten
records.category: supervisory failure at a collapsed commercial bank
records.people: Centrale Bank van Curaçao en Sint Maarten (CBCS); Girobank and its Supervisory Board (RvC); International Investment Group (IIG). No individuals are named on the page.
records.summary: In a presentation to the Parliament of Curaçao on December 4 (the article carries the byline date December 10, 2024; the page does not print the year of the presentation itself), the CBCS disclosed that inadequate oversight by the central bank was a significant factor in Girobank's downfall: it acknowledged that the 2010 acquisition of Girobank by the International Investment Group was vetted without proper scrutiny of the source of capital, conflicts of interest or the reliability of the new executives, that weak vetting let conflicts of interest involving Girobank's CEO go unnoticed, that it then failed to monitor the bank adequately as it issued high-risk loans, and that its delayed intervention made the crisis worse. The collapse required a 170-million-guilder loan from the Netherlands to compensate 98% of depositors.
records.detail: This is the central bank as the subject of the finding, not as detector: the failure disclosed is the CBCS's own supervision, admitted by the CBCS itself before Parliament, and it is distinct from both records the map already holds for Curaçao — the Emsley Tromp and Rene Laurents convictions (index 18) and the Algemene Rekenkamer's finding on 700 million in unlawful state loans where the Minister of Finance is the subject (index 283). The page also names a 2013 emergency regulation and a 2019 moratorium as the intervention measures that did not prevent the collapse. Every year and figure in this record is printed on the page at source_url; no date has been derived.
records.quote: the CBCS admitted that its initial oversight failed to prevent or mitigate the worsening crisis
records.source_title: Poor oversight by Central Bank led to Girobank crisis — Curaçao Chronicle, 10 December 2024
records.weak_source_note: The source is a local news outlet (Curaçao Chronicle) reporting a CBCS presentation to Parliament; the CBCS's own presentation document was not located, so this record rests on press reporting of it rather than on the primary document.

blanks.note: Banque Centrale de la République de Guinée, 'Rapport du commissaire aux comptes sur les états financiers, Exercice clos le 31 décembre 2023', signed by KPMG S.A. (Paris la Défense), downloaded in full from https://www.bcrg-guinee.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/BCRG-Rapport-audit-des-etats-financiers-au-31122023.pdf (758,524 bytes, 35,132 characters of extracted text) and read end to end. The opinion is UNMODIFIED: 'les états financiers ci-joints présentent sincèrement, dans tous leurs aspects significatifs, le patrimoine et la situation financière de l'Entité au 31 décembre 2023'. The statements were approved by the Governor on 18 septembre 2025. The report carries exactly one 'Observation' section, on the uncertainty disclosed in Note 5, and it explicitly states 'Notre opinion n'est pas modifiée à l'égard de ce point'. Note 5 ('OR ET ARGENT MONETAIRES') records that a technical gold-processing provider holding 3.1 tonnes (100,950.47 ounces) at 31 December 2023 has defaulted on returning the deposit since January 2022, that an ICC Paris arbitration gave an award in the Bank's favour in September 2024, and that a provision of 888.51 billion GNF (50% of fair value) was maintained. THAT IS THE BANK AS VICTIM, not as subject of wrongdoing, so it is refused as a case under the brief's rule on an outsider defrauding the bank. So: a clean audit opinion and no finding against the bank. Guinea's single record remains the 2026 conviction of former governor Ibrahima Chérif Bah. The Cour des comptes de Guinée was NOT reached: the French search returned no cour-des-comptes document at all, only BCRG and IMF material, so that institution is still untested.

Bank of Jamaica Annual Report 2025, the exact document round 72 named as the untested lead, downloaded in full from https://boj.org.jm/2025-boj-annual-report-final (33,617,846 bytes, 391,396 characters of extracted text; the 2024 report at /2024-boj-annual-report-final also returns HTTP 200 at 32,401,816 bytes and was not needed) and grepped in full for disciplin|misconduct|fraud|integrity|whistle|investigat|irregular|theft|embezzl|code of conduct|sanction. There is NO internal disciplinary or integrity finding against the Bank or its staff anywhere in it. Every hit is one of three things: fiscal discipline in the macroeconomic chapters; the external auditor's standard ISA boilerplate on misstatement arising from fraud or error (lines 7550-7575); or the Office of the Consumer Complaints Commissioner's statistics on complaints about SUPERVISED institutions — 93 fraud/impropriety complaints in 2025 against 103 in 2024, and a December 2025 spike in RTGS complaints which the report says 'was an exceptional issue and not evidence of systemic misconduct'. Those are the bank as supervisor and detector, not as subject. So the bank's-own-annual-report vein is read and empty for Jamaica, which with round 71's and 72's findings (the Auditor General's Department publishes nothing on the Bank of Jamaica, whose accounts are audited by private firms) leaves only the parliamentary route at japarliament.gov.jm, which was NOT reached this round.

FILED above from a different route, but recording the audit vein honestly. The PwC investigation report on the CBCS that round 72 named as the strongest untested Curaçao document is GONE from its host: https://knipselkrant-curacao.com//wp-content/uploads/2015/01/Rapport-PWC-Centrale-Bank-CBCS-Samenvatting-final-draftaan-JardimHassink.pdf (the exact URL, confirmed by a fresh search) now returns HTTP 404 with a 142,531-byte HTML error page — which is the same byte count round 72 recorded as a 'downloaded PDF', so round 72 never had the report either: it had the host's error page, and the 'scan that extracts zero characters' was HTML. pdftotext confirms it is not a PDF ('May not be a PDF file', illegal characters, no trailer dictionary). Do not spend another round on OCRing it. The Algemene Rekenkamer Curaçao's report on the Government's 2023 annual accounts remains unopened.

Searched in English for a Da Afghanistan Bank official convicted of or investigated for embezzlement of central bank funds. Every result returned is the Kabul Bank episode: the 2013 Kabul Bank Tribunal sentences on Sherkhan Farnood and Khalilullah Ferozi (Al Jazeera, Fox News, OCCRP, Afghanistan Analysts Network), the 900-million-dollar independent forensic report, New Kabul Bank, and Farnood's death in prison in 2018. Those are officers of a COMMERCIAL bank, not of Da Afghanistan Bank, and the one Afghan record the map holds (index 0) is already the official finding against DAB's supervisors over that same Kabul Bank collapse, 2004-2010. So there is no second Afghan episode on this search, and anything from these results would be the same episode in different words. Afghanistan's supreme audit institution was not reached and, given the 2021 change of government, was not pursued.

Searched in Spanish for a Contraloría General de la República de Cuba audit or report on the Banco Central de Cuba. The search returned no contraloria.gob.cu document and nothing naming the Banco Central de Cuba as an audited entity: what came back was Gaceta Oficial PDFs on cibercuba.com, a dozen Cubanet and 14ymedio pieces on the Contraloría's enterprise audits in general ('la corrupción azota a las empresas cubanas', 'la Contraloría cubana admite no consigue frenar la corrupción', 'aparatoso despliegue de auditores'), and an OnCuba report of a Havana audit finding 'daños millonarios por infracciones y negligencias' at unnamed entities. Round 71's standing note is therefore confirmed by search rather than merely assumed: the Contraloría does not publish per-entity audit reports, and no Cuban audit document naming the central bank is reachable. Cuba's single record remains the 2026 Santiago de Cuba cash-for-transfer investigation at two state bank branches.

Third consecutive round in which the Cámara de Cuentas de la República Dominicana's own publications index could not be reached, and the reason is now established rather than guessed: a Spanish search aimed squarely at the host ('camaradecuentas.gob.do informes de auditoría publicados listado entidades') returned NO camaradecuentas.gob.do URL at all — nineteen results, every one of them press coverage (El Nuevo Diario, CDN, El Caribe, El Día, Diario Libre) of audits the Cámara has approved, plus the Cámara de Diputados' own copy of the audit report on itself and a Contraloría analysis PDF. The entities named across that coverage are SENASA, Promipyme, Banca Solidaria, CODIA, INDOTEL, PROMESE, Medio Ambiente, APORDOM, Tamayo, the Cámara de Diputados and COVID aid programmes; the Banco Central de la República Dominicana appears nowhere. Recommendation for the next round: do not spend another search on this host via a search engine — it does not surface. The country's one record (index 199, the Malkún charges) stands.

Partly advanced, not closed. The Ríkisendurskoðun report index at https://www.rikisendurskodun.is/skyrslur was re-fetched (45,582 bytes) and its filter vocabulary extracted in full, which round 72 did not have: searchString2 takes 0 'Allt útgefið efni', 1 'Endurskoðunarskýrsla', 2 'Skýrsla til Alþingis', 4 'Staðfestir sjóðir og stofnanir', 5 'Kirkjugarðar og sóknir', 6 'Stjórnmálastarfsemi', 7 'Almennt'; searchString1 is a year list running 1988 to 2026. So the unenumerated categories are 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7, not just 2. The index uses next-page pagination (only pageIndex=2 appears in the markup) over detail links /skyrslur/nanar?id=NNNN running down from id=2087, so the whole corpus is on the order of 2,000 items and enumerating 'Allt útgefið efni' is not affordable within a 25-fetch budget. A separate attempt at a second Icelandic episode — the Central Bank's capital-controls case against Samherji — was searched and NOT filed: the only substantive sources are Samherji's own website (an interested party to the dispute) and a Central Banking piece on the bank's dawn raid, which is the bank as enforcer; cb.is's 2 May 2019 item is a departmental reorganisation and states no finding. Iceland's one record remains the 2010 Special Investigation Commission finding.

The standing lead could not be opened for a host reason, not a content reason. An Arabic search for ديوان المحاسبة reporting on the البنك المركزي الأردني returned two Audit Bureau PDFs on the government portal, https://portal.jordan.gov.jo/OD/files/1048.pdf and /2413.pdf, plus Al-Mamlaka TV coverage of the Audit Bureau report ('الرزاز لا تهاون مع مخالفات تقرير ديوان المحاسبة', 'الصفدي يتسلم تقرير ديوان المحاسبة') and a Chamber of Deputies session agenda. portal.jordan.gov.jo:443 failed four times through the agent proxy with ws_closed_mid_exchange (HTTP 000, 0 bytes) and was never reached, so nothing about Jordan was tested. Named for the next round, with the URLs now in hand: portal.jordan.gov.jo/OD/files/1048.pdf and /2413.pdf, to be tried with WebFetch rather than curl, and the Chamber of Deputies site representatives.jo, whose session agendas are served as PDF. Jordan's single record is still the Wikipedia-sourced Petra Bank / Chalabi case, so an Audit Bureau finding would both add an episode and replace a weak source.

So the Burundian supreme-audit vein is not shown absent, it is simply not served by search, and the BRB's own annual report governance section was not opened (round 72 recorded that bcb.bi returns HTTP 429 to curl and needs WebFetch). Burundi's one case and one event are the same episode — the October 2023 prosecution and dismissal of governor Dieudonné Murengerantwari — so a second must be an unrelated episode.
